entries.3b74dc7520bc8ddf5ef3f5bbb9ae1a7c89ec7f44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv123"/><title type="x-ms">Titus</title> <div sID="gen32585" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32585" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s4">Completed by <hi type="small-caps">Jeremiah Smith</hi> .</title> <div sID="gen32586" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> Epistle of Paul to Titus is much of the same nature with those to Timothy; both were converts of Paul, and his companions in labours and sufferings; both were in the office of evangelists, whose work was to water the churches planted by the apostles, and to set in order the things that were wanting in them: they were vice-apostles, as it were, <hi type="italic">working the work of the Lord, as they did,</hi> and mostly under their direction, though not despotic and arbitrary, but with the concurring exercise of their own prudence and judgment, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1 Cor. xvi. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.12">12</reference>. We read much of this Titus, his titles, character, and active usefulness, in many places—he was a Greek, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.3">Gal. ii. 3</reference>. Paul called him <hi type="italic">his son</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.4">Tit. i. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">his brother</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">2 Cor. ii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">his partner and fellow-helper</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">2 Cor. viii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">one that walked in the same spirit and in the same steps with himself.</hi> He went up with the apostles to the church at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.1">Gal. ii. 1</reference>), was much conversant at Corinth, for which church he had <hi type="italic">an earnest care,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16">2 Cor. viii. 16</reference>. Paul's second epistle to them, and probably his first also, was sent by his hand, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16-2Cor.8.18 2Cor.8.23 2Cor.9.2-2Cor.9.4 2Cor.12.18">2 Cor. viii. 16-18, 23; ix. 2-4; xii. 18</reference>. He was with the apostle at Rome, and thence went into Dalmatia (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2 Tim. iv. 10</reference>), after which no more occurs of him in the scriptures. So that by them he appears not to have been a fixed bishop; if such he were, and in those times, the church of Corinth, where he most laboured, had the best title to him. In Crete (now called <hi type="italic">Candia,</hi> formerly <hi type="italic">Hecatompolis,</hi> from the hundred cities that were in it), a large island at the mouth of the Ægean Sea, the gospel had got some footing; and here were Paul and Titus in one of their travels, cultivating this plantation; but the apostle of the Gentiles, having on him the care of all the churches, could not himself tarry long at this place. He therefore left Titus some time there, to carry on the work which had been begun, wherein, probably, meeting with more difficulty than ordinary, Paul wrote this epistle to him; and yet perhaps not so much for his own sake as for the people's, that the endeavours of Titus, strengthened with apostolic advice and authority, might be more significant and effectual among them. He was to see all the cities furnished with good pastors, to reject and keep out the unmeet and unworthy, to teach sound doctrine, and instruct all sorts in their duties, to set forth the free grace of God in man's salvation by Christ, and withal to show the necessity of maintaining good works by those who have believed in God and hope for eternal life from him. <div eID="gen32586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32587" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32588" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The preface or introduction to the epistle, showing from and to whom it was written, with the apostle's salutation and prayer for Titus, wishing all blessings to him, <reference osisRef="Titus.1.1-Titus.1.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. Entrance into the matter, by signifying the end of Titus's being left at Crete, <reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">ver. 5</reference>. III. And how the same should be pursued in reference both to good and bad ministers, <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6-Titus.1.16">ver. 6, to the end</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv123"/> <div eID="gen32588" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32587" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Introduction; The Apostle's Charge to Titus. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32589" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness; <hi type="super">2</hi> In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began; <hi type="super">3</hi> But hath in due times manifested his word through preaching, which is committed unto me according to the commandment of God our Saviour; <hi type="super">4</hi> To Titus, <hi type="italic">mine</hi> own son after the common faith: Grace, mercy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour. <div eID="gen32589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32590" type="x-p"/> Here is the preface to the epistle, showing, <div eID="gen32590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32591" type="x-p"/> I. The writer. <hi type="italic">Paul,</hi> a Gentile name taken by the apostle of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.9">Acts xiii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.46">46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.47">47</reference>. Ministers will accommodate even smaller matters, so that they may be any furthering of acceptance in their work. When the Jews rejected the gospel, and the Gentiles received it, we read no more of this apostle by his Jewish name <hi type="italic">Saul,</hi> but by his Roman one, <hi type="italic">Paul. A servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ.</hi> Here he is described by his relation and office: <hi type="italic">A servant of God,</hi> not in the general sense only, as a man and a Christian, but especially as a minister, <hi type="italic">serving God in the gospel of his Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Rom. i. 9</reference>. This is a high honour; it is the glory of angels that they are <hi type="italic">ministering spirits, and sent forth to minister for those who shall be heirs of salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">Heb. i. 14</reference>. Paul is described more especially as a chief minister, <hi type="italic">an apostle of Jesus Christ;</hi> one who had seen the Lord, and was immediately called and commissioned by him, and had his doctrine from him. Observe, The highest officers in the church are but servants. (Much divinity and devotion are comprehended in the inscriptions of the epistles.) The apostles of Jesus Christ, who were employed to spread and propagate his religion, were therein also the servants of God; they did not set up any thing inconsistent with the truths and duties of natural religion. Christianity, which they preached, was in order to clear and enforce those natural principles, as well as to advance them, and to superadd what was fit and necessary in man's degenerate and revolted state: therefore the apostles of Jesus Christ were the servants of God, <hi type="italic">according to the faith of God's elect.</hi> Their doctrine agreed with the faith of all the elect from the beginning of the world, and was for propagating and promoting the same. Observe, There are elect of God (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1 Pet. i. 2</reference>), and in these the Holy Spirit works precious divine faith, proper to those who are chosen to eternal life (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13-2Thess.2.14">2 Thess. ii. 13, 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation, through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth, whereunto he called you by our gospel.</hi> Faith is the first principle of sanctification. <hi type="italic">And the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness.</hi> The gospel is truth; the great, sure, and saving truth (<reference osisRef="Col.1.5">Col. i. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">the word of the truth of the gospel.</hi> Divine faith rests not on fallible reasonings and probable opinions, but on the infallible word, the truth itself, <hi type="italic">which is after godliness,</hi> of a godly nature and tendency, pure, and purifying the heart of the believer. By this mark judge of doctrines and of spirits—whether they be of God or not; what is impure, and prejudicial to true piety and practical religion, cannot be of divine original. All gospel truth is after godliness, teaching and nourishing reverence and fear of God, and obedience to him; it is truth not only to be known, but acknowledged; it must be held forth in word and practice, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.15-Phil.2.16">Phil. ii. 15, 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">With the heart man believes to righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.10">Rom. x. 10</reference>. Such as retain the truth in unrighteousness neither know nor believe as they ought. To bring to this knowledge and faith, and to the acknowledging and professing of the truth which is after godliness, is the great end of the gospel ministry, even of the highest degree and order in it; their teachings should have this chief aim, to beget faith and confirm in it. <hi type="italic">In</hi> (or<hi type="italic">for</hi>) <hi type="italic">hope of eternal life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">v. 2</reference>. This is the further intent of the gospel, to beget hope as well as faith; to take off the mind and heart from the world, and to raise them to heaven and the things above. The faith and godliness of Christians lead to eternal life, and give hope and well-grounded expectation of it; for <hi type="italic">God, that cannot lie, hath promised it.</hi> It is the honour of God that he cannot lie or deceive: and this is the comfort of believers, whose treasure is laid up in his faithful promises. But how is he said to promise before the world began? <hi type="italic">Answer,</hi> By promise some understand his decree: he purposed it in his eternal counsels, which were as it were his promise in <hi type="italic">embryo:</hi> or rather, say some, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pro chronon aionion</hi></hi> is <hi type="italic">before ancient times,</hi> or many years ago, referring to the promise darkly delivered, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>. Here is the stability and antiquity of the promise of eternal life to the saints. God, who cannot lie, hath promised before the world began, that is, many ages since. How excellent then is the gospel, which was the matter of divine promise so early! how much to be esteemed by us, and what thanks due for our privilege beyond those before us! <hi type="italic">Blessed are your eyes, for they see,</hi> &c. No wonder if the contempt of it be punished severely, since he has not only promised it of old, <hi type="italic">but</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">v. 3</reference>) <hi type="italic">has in due times manifested his word through preaching;</hi> that is, made that his promise, so darkly delivered of old, <hi type="italic">in due time</hi> (the proper season before appointed) more plain <hi type="italic">by preaching;</hi> that which some called <hi type="italic">foolishness of preaching</hi> has been thus honoured. <hi type="italic">Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God,</hi> by the word preached. <hi type="italic">Which is committed unto me.</hi> The ministry is a trust; none taketh this honour, but he who is thereunto appointed; and whoso is appointed and called must preach the word. <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.16">1 Cor. ix. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">Woe is unto me if I preach not the gospel.</hi> Nonpreaching ministers are none of the apostle's successors. <hi type="italic">According to the commandment of God our Saviour.</hi> Preaching is a work appointed by a God as a Saviour. See a proof here of Christ's deity, for by him was the gospel committed to Paul when he was converted (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.15 Acts.9.17 Acts.22.10 Acts.22.14 Acts.22.15">Acts ix. 15, 17, and ch. xxii. 10, 14, 15</reference>), and again when Christ appeared to him, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.17-Acts.22.21">v. 17-21</reference>. He therefore is this Saviour; not but that the whole Timothy concur therein: the Father saves by the Son through the Spirit, and all concur in sending ministers. Let none rest therefore in men's calling, without God's; he furnishes, inclines, authorizes, and gives opportunity for the work. <div eID="gen32591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32592" type="x-p"/> II. The person written to, who is described, 1. By his name, <hi type="italic">Titus,</hi> a Gentile Greek, yet called both to the faith and ministry. Observe, the grace of God is free and powerful. What worthiness or preparation was there in one of heathen stock and education? 2. By his spiritual relation to the apostle: <hi type="italic">My own</hi> (or <hi type="italic">my genuine</hi>) <hi type="italic">son,</hi> not by natural generation, but by supernatural regeneration. <hi type="italic">I have begotten you through the gospel,</hi> said he to the Corinthians, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">1 Cor. iv. 15</reference>. Ministers are spiritual fathers to those whom they are the means of converting, and will tenderly affect and care for them, and must be answerably regarded by them. "<hi type="italic">My own son after the common faith,</hi> that faith which is common to all the regenerate, and which thou hast in truth, and expressest to the life." This might be said to distinguish Titus from hypocrites and false teachers, and to recommend him to the regard of the Cretans, as being among them a lively image of the apostle himself, in faith, and life, and heavenly doctrine. To this Titus, deservedly so dear to the apostle, is, <div eID="gen32592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32593" type="x-p"/> III. The salutation and prayer, wishing all blessings to him: <hi type="italic">Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour.</hi> Here are, 1. The blessings wished: <hi type="italic">Grace, mercy, and peace. Grace,</hi> the free favour of God, and acceptance with him. <hi type="italic">Mercy,</hi> the fruits of that favour, in pardon of sins, and freedom from all miseries by it, both here and hereafter. And <hi type="italic">peace,</hi> the positive effect and fruit of mercy. Peace with God through Christ who is our peace, and with the creatures and ourselves; outward and inward peace, comprehending all good whatsoever, that makes for our happiness in time and to eternity. Observe, Grace is the fountain of all blessings. Mercy, and peace, and all good, spring out of this. Get into God's favour, and all must be well; for, 2. These are the persons from whom blessings are wished: <hi type="italic">From God the Father,</hi> the fountain of all good. Every blessing, every comfort, comes to us from God as a Father; he is the Father of all by creation, but of the good by adoption and regeneration. <hi type="italic">And the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour,</hi> as the way and means of procurement and conveyance. All is from the Father by the Son, who is Lord by nature, heir of all things, and our Lord, Redeemer, and head, ordering and ruling his members. All are put under him; we hold of him, as <hi type="italic">in capite,</hi> and owe subjection and obedience to him, who is also Jesus and Christ, the anointed Saviour, and especially our Saviour, who believe in him, delivering us from sin and hell, and bringing us to heaven and happiness. <div eID="gen32593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32594" type="x-p"/> Thus far is the preface to the epistle; then follows the entrance into the matter, by signifying the end of Titus's being left in Crete.
entries.1bab0b0ddde70c1ec5856099d59ea52f460e258f: <div eID="gen32594" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ordination of Elders. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32595" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee: <div eID="gen32595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32596" type="x-p"/> Here is the end expressed, <div eID="gen32596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32597" type="x-p"/> I. More generally: <hi type="italic">For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldst set in order the things that are wanting.</hi> This was the business of evangelists (in which office Titus was), to water where the apostles had planted (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1 Cor. iii. 6</reference>), furthering and finishing what they had begun; so much <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epidiorthoun</hi></hi> imports, <hi type="italic">to order after another.</hi> Titus was to go on in settling what the apostle himself had not time for, in his short stay there. Observe, 1. The apostle's great diligence in the gospel; when he had set things on foot in one place, he hastened away to another. He was debtor to the Greeks and to the barbarians, and laboured to spread the gospel as far as he could among them all. And, 2. His faithfulness and prudence. He neglected not the places that he went from; but left some to cultivate the young plantation, and carry on what was begun. 3. His humility; he disdained not to be helped in his work, and that by such as were not of so high a rank in the ministry, nor of so great gifts and furniture, as himself; so that the gospel might be furthered and the good of souls promoted, he willingly used the hands of others in it: a fit example for exciting zeal and industry, and engaging to faithfulness and care of the flock, and present or absent, living and dying, for ministers, as much as in them lies, to provide for the spiritual edification and comfort of their people. We may here also observe, 4. That Titus, though inferior to an apostle, was yet above the ordinary fixed pastors or bishops, who were to tend particular churches as their peculiar stated charge; but Titus was in a higher sphere, to ordain such ordinary pastors where wanting, and settle things in their first state and form, and then to pass to other places for like service as there might be need. Titus was not only a minister of the catholic church (as all others also are), but a catholic minister. Others had power habitual, and in <hi type="italic">actu primo,</hi> to minister any where, upon call and opportunity; but evangelists, such as Titus was, had power in <hi type="italic">actu secundo et exercito,</hi> and could exercise their ministry wherever they came, and claim maintenance of the churches. They were every where actually in their diocese or province, and had a right to direct and preside among the ordinary pastors and ministers. Where an apostle could act as an apostle an evangelist could act as an evangelist; for <hi type="italic">they worked the work of the Lord as they did</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1 Cor. xvi. 10</reference>), in a like unfixed and itinerant manner. Here at Crete Titus was but occasionally, and for a short time; Paul willed him to despatch the business he was left for, and come to him at Nicopolis, where he purposed to winter; after this he was sent to Corinth, was with the apostle at Rome, and was sent thence into Dalmatia, which is the last we read of him in scripture, so that from scripture no fixed episcopacy in him does appear; he left Crete, and we find not that he returned thither any more. But what power had either Paul or Titus here? Was not what they did an encroachment on the rights of civil rulers? In no sort; they came not to meddle with the civil rights of any. <reference osisRef="Luke.12.14">Luke xii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Who made me a judge or a divider over you?</hi> Their work was spiritual, to be carried on by conviction and persuasion, no way interfering with, or prejudicing, or weakening, the power of magistrates, but rather securing and strengthening it; the <hi type="italic">things wanting</hi> were not such as civil magistrates are the fountains or authors of, but divine and spiritual ordinances, and appointments for spiritual ends, derived from Christ the king and head of the church: for settling these was Titus left. And observe, No easy thing is it to raise churches, and bring them to perfection. Paul had himself been here labouring, and yet were there things wanting; materials are out of square, need much hewing and fitting, to bring them into right form, and, when they are set therein, to hold and keep them so. The best are apt to decay and to go out of order. Ministers are to help against this, to get what is amiss rectified, and what is wanting supplied. This in general was Titus's work in Crete: and, <div eID="gen32597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32598" type="x-p"/> II. In special: <hi type="italic">To ordain elders in every city,</hi> that is, ministers, who were mostly out of the elder and most understanding and experienced Christians; or, if younger in years, yet such as were grave and solid in their deportment and manners. These were to be set where there was any fit number of Christians, as in larger towns and cities was usually the case; though villages, too, might have them where there were Christians enough for it. These presbyters or elders were to have the ordinary and stated care and charge of the churches; to feed and govern them, and perform all pastoral work and duty in and towards them. The word is used sometimes more largely for any who bear ecclesiastical function in the church, and so the apostles were <hi type="italic">presbyters</hi> or <hi type="italic">elders</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1">1 Pet. v. 1</reference>); but here it is meant of ordinary fixed pastors, who <hi type="italic">laboured in the word and doctrine,</hi> and were <hi type="italic">over the churches in the Lord;</hi> such as are described here throughout the chapter. This word <hi type="italic">presbyter</hi> some use in the same sense as <hi type="italic">sacerdos,</hi> and translate it <hi type="italic">priest,</hi> a term not given to gospel ministers, unless in a figurative or allusive way, as all God's people are said to be made <hi type="italic">kings and priests unto God</hi> (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hiereis,</hi></hi> not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">presbyterous</hi></hi>), to offer up spiritual sacrifices of prayers, praises, and alms. But properly we have no priest under the gospel, except Christ alone, <hi type="italic">the high priest of our profession</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.1">Heb. iii. 1</reference>), who offered up himself a sacrifice to God for us, and ever lives, in virtue thereof, to make intercession in our behalf. Presbyters here therefore are not proper priests, to offer sacrifices, either typical or real; but only gospel ministers, to dispense Christ's ordinances, and to <hi type="italic">feed the church of God, over which the Holy Ghost has made them overseers.</hi> Observe, 1. A church without a fixed and standing ministry in it is imperfect and wanting. 2. Where a fit number of believers is, presbyters or elders must be set; their continuance in churches is as necessary as their first appointment, <hi type="italic">for perfecting the saints, and edifying the body of Christ, till all come to a perfect man in Christ,</hi> till the whole number of God's chosen be called and united to Christ in one body, and brought to their full stature and strength, and that measure of grace that is proper and designed for them, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.12-Eph.4.13">Eph. iv. 12, 13</reference>. This is work that must and will be doing to the world's end, to which therefore the necessary and appointed means for it must last. What praise is due to God for such an institution! What thankfulness from those that enjoy the benefits of it! What pity and prayer for such as want it! <hi type="italic">Pray the Lord of the harvest that he will send forth labourers into his harvest. Faith comes by hearing,</hi> and is preserved, maintained, and made fruitful, through it also. Ignorance and corruption, decays of good and increase of all evil, come by want of a teaching and quickening ministry. On such accounts therefore was <hi type="italic">Titus left in Crete, to set in order the things that were wanting, and to ordain elders in every city;</hi> but this he was to do, not <hi type="italic">ad libitum,</hi> or according to his own will or fancy, but according to apostolic direction. <div eID="gen32598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32599" type="x-p"/> III. The rule of his proceeding: <hi type="italic">As I had appointed thee,</hi> probably when he was going from him, and in the presence and hearing of others, to which he may now refer, not so much for Titus's own sake as for the people's, that they might the more readily yield obedience to Titus, knowing and observing that in what he did he was warranted and supported by apostolic injunction and authority. As under the law all things were to be made according to the pattern shown to Moses in the mount; so under the gospel all must be ordered and managed according to the direction of Christ, and of his chief ministers, who were infallibly guided by him. Human traditions and inventions may not be brought into the church of God. Prudent disposals for carrying on the ends of Christ's appointments, according to the general rules of the word, there may, yea, must be; but none may alter any thing in the substance of the faith or worship, or order and discipline, of the churches. If an evangelist might not do any thing but by appointment, much less may others. The church is the house of God, and to him it belongs to appoint the officers and orders of it, as he pleases: the <hi type="italic">as</hi> here refers to the qualifications and character of the elders that he was to ordain: "<hi type="italic">Ordain elders in every city, as I appointed thee,</hi> such as I then described and shall now again more particularly point out to thee," which he does from the <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6-Titus.1.9">sixth verse to the ninth</reference> inclusive.
entries.0e3cfc431aa605b1bed2db72008deb4790b94d70: <div eID="gen32599" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Qualifications of a Bishop; The Necessity of Sharp Reproof. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32600" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly. <hi type="super">7</hi> For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre; <hi type="super">8</hi> But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate; <hi type="super">9</hi> Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers. 10 For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision: <hi type="super">11</hi> Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake. <hi type="super">12</hi> One of themselves, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a prophet of their own, said, The Cretians <hi type="italic">are</hi> alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies. <hi type="super">13</hi> This witness is true. Wherefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith; <hi type="super">14</hi> Not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth. <hi type="super">15</hi> Unto the pure all things <hi type="italic">are</hi> pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving <hi type="italic">is</hi> nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled. <hi type="super">16</hi> They profess that they know God; but in works they deny <hi type="italic">him,</hi> being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate. <div eID="gen32600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32601" type="x-p"/> The apostle here gives Titus directions about ordination, showing whom he should ordain, and whom not. <div eID="gen32601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32602" type="x-p"/> I. Of those whom he should ordain. He points out their qualifications and virtues; such as respect their life and manners, and such as relate to their doctrine: the former in the <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6-Titus.1.8">sixth, seventh, and eighth verses</reference>, and the latter in the <reference osisRef="Titus.1.9">ninth</reference>. <div eID="gen32602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32603" type="x-p"/> 1. Their qualifications respecting their life and manners are, <div eID="gen32603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32604" type="x-p"/> (1.) More general: <hi type="italic">If any be blameless;</hi> not absolutely without fault, so none are, for <hi type="italic">there is none that liveth and sinneth not;</hi> nor altogether unblamed, this is rare and difficult. Christ himself and his apostles were blamed, though not worthy of it. In Christ thee was certainly nothing blamable; and his apostles were not such as their enemies charged them to be. But the meaning is, He must be one who lies not under an ill character; but rather must have good report, even <hi type="italic">from those that are without;</hi> not grossly or scandalously guilty, so as would bring reproach upon the holy function; he must not be such a one. <div eID="gen32604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32605" type="x-p"/> (2.) More particularly. <div eID="gen32605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32606" type="x-p"/> [1.] There is his relative character. In his own person, he must be of conjugal chastity: <hi type="italic">The husband of one wife.</hi> The church of Rome says the husband of <hi type="italic">no</hi> wife, but from the beginning it was not so; marriage is an ordinance from which no profession nor calling is a bar. <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.5">1 Cor. ix. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Have I not power,</hi> says Paul, <hi type="italic">to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles? Forbidding to marry</hi> is one of the erroneous doctrines of the antichristian church, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1 Tim. iv. 3</reference>. Not that ministers <hi type="italic">must</hi> be married; this is not meant; but <hi type="italic">the husband of one wife</hi> may be either not having divorced his wife and married another (as was too common among those of the circumcision, even for slight causes), or <hi type="italic">the husband of one wife,</hi> that is, at one and the same time, no bigamist; not that he might not be married to more than one wife successively, but, being married, he must have but one wife at once, not two or more, according to the too common sinful practice of those times, by a perverse imitation of the patriarchs, from which evil custom our Lord taught a reformation. Polygamy is scandalous in any, as also having a harlot or concubine with his lawful wife; such sin, or any wanton libidinous demeanour, must be very remote from such as would enter into so sacred a function. And, as to his children, <hi type="italic">having faithful children,</hi> obedient and good, brought up in the true Christian faith, and living according to it, at least as far as the endeavours of the parents can avail. It is for the honour of ministers that their children be faithful and pious, and such as become their religion. <hi type="italic">Not accused of riot, nor unruly,</hi> not justly so accused, as having given ground and occasion for it, for otherwise the most innocent may be falsely so charged; they must look to it therefore that there be no colour for such censure. Children so faithful, and obedient, and temperate, will be a good sign of faithfulness and diligence in the parent who has so educated and instructed them; and, from his faithfulness in the less, there may be encouragement to commit to him the greater, the rule and government of the church of God. The ground of this qualification is shown from the nature of his office (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God.</hi> Those before termed presbyters, or elders, are in this verse styled bishops; and such they were, having no ordinary fixed and standing officers above them. Titus's business here, it is plain, was but occasional, and his stay short, as was before noted. Having ordained elders, and settled in their due form, he went and left all (for aught that appears in scripture) in the hands of those elders whom the apostle here calls bishops and stewards of God. We read not in the sacred writings of any successor he had in Crete; but to those elders or bishops was committed the full charge of feeding, ruling, and watching over their flock; they wanted not any powers necessary for carrying on religion and the ministry of it among them, and committing it down to succeeding ages. Now, being such bishops and overseers of the flock, who were to be examples to them, and God's stewards to take care of the affairs of his house, to provide for and dispense to them things needful, there is great reason that their character should be clear and good, that they should be blameless. How else could it be but that religion must suffer, their work be hindered, and souls prejudiced and endangered, whom they were set to save? These are the relative qualifications with the ground of them. <div eID="gen32606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32607" type="x-p"/> [2.] The more absolute ones are expressed, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Negatively, showing what an elder or bishop must not be: <hi type="italic">Not self-willed.</hi> The prohibition is of large extent, excluding self-opinion, or overweening conceit of parts and abilities, and abounding in one's own sense,—self-love, and self-seeking, making self the centre of all,—also self-confidence and trust, and self-pleasing, little regarding or setting by others,—being proud, stubborn, froward, inflexible, set on one's own will and way, or churlish as Nabal: such is the sense expositors have affixed to the term. A great honour it is to a minister not to be thus affected, to be ready to ask and to take advice, to be ready to defer as much as reasonably may be to the mind and will of others, becoming all things to all men, that they may gain some. <hi type="italic">Not soon angry,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me orgilon,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">not one of a hasty angry temper,</hi> soon and easily provoked and inflamed. How unfit are those to govern a church who cannot govern themselves, or their own turbulent and unruly passions! The minister must be meek and gentle, and patient towards all men. <hi type="italic">Not given to wine;</hi> thee is no greater reproach on a minister than to be a wine-bibber, one who loves it, and gives himself undue liberty this way who <hi type="italic">continues at the wine or strong drink till it inflames him.</hi> Seasonable and moderate use of this, as of the other good creatures of God, is not unlawful. <hi type="italic">Use a little wine for thy stomach's sake, and thine often infirmities,</hi> said Paul to Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1 Tim. v. 23</reference>. But excess therein is shameful in all, especially in a minister. <hi type="italic">Wine takes away the heart,</hi> turns the man into a brute: here most proper is that exhortation of the apostle (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.18">Eph. v. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.</hi> Here is no exceeding, but in the former too easily there may: take heed therefore of going too near the brink. <hi type="italic">No striker,</hi> in any quarrelsome or contentious manner, not injuriously nor out of revenge, with cruelty or unnecessary roughness. <hi type="italic">Not given to filthy lucre;</hi> not greedy of it (as <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1 Tim. iii. 3</reference>), whereby is not meant refusing a just return for their labours, in order to their necessary support and comfort; but not making gain their first or chief end, not entering into the ministry nor managing it with base worldly views. Nothing is more unbecoming a minister, who is to direct his own and others' eyes to another world, than to be too intent upon this. It is called <hi type="italic">filthy lucre,</hi> from its defiling the soul that inordinately affects or greedily looks after it, as if it were any otherwise desirable than for the good and lawful uses of it. Thus of the negative part of the bishop's character. But, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Positively: he must be (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.8">v. 8</reference>) <hi type="italic">a lover of hospitality,</hi> as an evidence that he is not given to filthy lucre, but is willing to use what he has to the best purposes, not laying up for himself, so as to hinder charitable laying out for the good of others; <hi type="italic">receiving and entertaining strangers</hi> (as the word imports), a great and necessary office of love, especially in those times of affliction and distress, when Christians were made to fly and wander for safety from persecution and enemies, or in travelling to and fro where there were not such public houses for reception as in our days, nor, it may be, had many poor saints sufficiency of their own for such uses—then to receive and entertain them was good and pleasing to God. And such a spirit and practice, according to ability and occasion, are very becoming such as should be examples of good works. <hi type="italic">A lover of good men,</hi> or of <hi type="italic">good things;</hi> ministers should be exemplary in both; this will evince their open piety, and likeness to God and their Master Jesus Christ: <hi type="italic">Do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith,</hi> those who are the excellent of the earth, in whom should be all our delight. <hi type="italic">Sober,</hi> or <hi type="italic">prudent,</hi> as the word signifies; a needful grace in a minister both for his ministerial and personal carriage and management. He should be a wise steward, and one who is not rash, or foolish, or heady; but who can govern well his passions and affections. <hi type="italic">Just</hi> in things belonging to civil life, and moral righteousness, and equity in dealings, giving to all their due. <hi type="italic">Holy,</hi> in what concerns religion; one who reverences and worships God, and is of a spiritual and heavenly conversation. <hi type="italic">Temperate;</hi> it comes from a word that signifies <hi type="italic">strength,</hi> and denotes one who has power over his appetite and affections, or, in things lawful, can, for good ends, restrain and hold them in. Nothing is more becoming a minister than such things as these, <hi type="italic">sobriety, temperance, justice,</hi> and <hi type="italic">holiness</hi>—sober in respect of himself, just and righteous towards all men, and holy towards God. And thus of the qualifications respecting the minister's life and manners, relative and absolute, negative and positive, what he must not, and what he must, be and do. <div eID="gen32607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32608" type="x-p"/> 2. As to doctrine, <div eID="gen32608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32609" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is his duty: <hi type="italic">Holding fast the faithful word, as he has been taught,</hi> keeping close to the doctrine of Christ, <hi type="italic">the word of his grace,</hi> adhering thereto according to the instructions he has received—holding it fast in his own belief and profession, and in teaching others. Observe, [1.] The word of God, revealed in the scripture, is a true and infallible word; the word of him that <hi type="italic">is the amen, the true and faithful witness,</hi> and whose Spirit guided the penmen of it. <hi type="italic">Holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.</hi> [2.] Ministers must hold fast, and hold forth, the faithful word in their teaching and life. <hi type="italic">I have kept the faith,</hi> was Paul's comfort (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7">2 Tim. iv. 7</reference>), and <hi type="italic">not shunned to declare the whole counsel of God;</hi> there was his faithfulness, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Acts xx. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen32609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32610" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is the end: <hi type="italic">That he may be able, by sound doctrine, both to exhort, and to convince the gainsayers,</hi> to persuade and draw others to the true faith, and to convince the contrary-minded. How should he do this if he himself were uncertain or unsteady, not holding fast that <hi type="italic">faithful word and sound doctrine</hi> which should be the matter of this teaching, and the means and ground of convincing those that oppose the truth? We see here summarily the great work of the ministry—to exhort those who are willing to know and do their duty, and to convince those that contradict, both which are to be done by <hi type="italic">sound doctrine,</hi> that is, in a rational instructive way, by scripture-arguments and testimonies, which are the infallible words of truth, what all may and should rest and be satisfied in and determined by. And thus of the qualifications of the elders whom Titus was to ordain. <div eID="gen32610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32611" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle's directory shows whom he should reject or avoid—men of another character, the mention of whom is brought in as a reason of the care he had recommended about the qualifications of ministers, why they should be such, and only such, as he had described. The reasons he takes both from bad teachers and hearers among them, <reference osisRef="Titus.1.10-Titus.1.16">v. 10, to the end</reference>. <div eID="gen32611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32612" type="x-p"/> 1. From bad teachers. (1.) Those false teachers are described. They were <hi type="italic">unruly,</hi> headstrong and ambitious of power, refractory and untractable (as some render it), and such as would not bear nor submit themselves to the discipline and necessary order in the church, impatient of good government and of sound doctrine. <hi type="italic">And vain talkers and deceivers,</hi> conceiting themselves to be wise, but really foolish, and thence great talkers, falling into errors and mistakes, and fond of them, and studious and industrious to draw others into the same. Many such there were, <hi type="italic">especially those of the circumcision,</hi> converts as they pretended, at least, from the Jews, who yet were for mingling Judaism and Christianity together, and so making a corrupt medley. These were the false teachers. (2.) Here is the apostle's direction how to deal with them (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their mouths must be stopped;</hi> not by outward force (Titus had no such power, nor was this the gospel method), but by confutation and conviction, showing them their error, <hi type="italic">not giving place to them even for an hour.</hi> In case of obstinacy indeed, breaking the peace of the church, and corrupting other churches, censures are to have place, the last means for recovering the faulty and preventing the hurt of many. Observe, Faithful ministers must oppose seducers in good time, <hi type="italic">that, their folly being made manifest, they may proceed no further.</hi> (3.) The reasons are given for this. [1.] From the pernicious effects of their errors: <hi type="italic">They subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not</hi> (namely, the necessity of circumcision, and of keeping the law of Moses, &c.), so subverting the gospel and the souls of men; not some few only, but whole families. It was unjustly charged on the apostles <hi type="italic">that they turned the world upside down;</hi> but justly on these false teachers that they drew many from the true faith to their ruin: the mouths of such should be stopped, especially considering, [2.] Their base end in what they do: <hi type="italic">For filthy lucre's sake,</hi> serving a worldly interest under pretence of religion. <hi type="italic">Love of money is the root of all evil.</hi> Most fit it is that such should be resisted, confuted, and put to shame, by sound doctrine, and reasons from the scriptures. Thus of the grounds respecting the bad teachers. <div eID="gen32612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32613" type="x-p"/> II. In reference to their people or hearers, who are described from ancient testimony given of them. <div eID="gen32613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32614" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is the witness (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">One of themselves, even a prophet of their own,</hi> that is, one of the Cretans, not of the Jews, Epimenides a Greek poet, likely to know and unlikely to slander them. <hi type="italic">A prophet of their own;</hi> so their poets were accounted, writers of divine oracles; these often witnessed against the vices of the people: Aratus, Epimenides, and others among the Greeks; Horace, Juvenal, and Persius, among the Latins: much smartness did they use against divers vices. <div eID="gen32614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32615" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the matter of his testimony: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kretes aei pseustai, kaka theria, gasteres argai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies.</hi> Even to a proverb, they were infamous for falsehood and lying; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kretizein,</hi></hi> to play the <hi type="italic">Cretan,</hi> or to lie, is the same; and they were compared to evil beasts for their sly hurtfulness and savage nature, and called slow bellies for their laziness and sensuality, more inclined to eat than to work and live by some honest employment. Observe, Such scandalous vices as were the reproach of heathens should be far from Christians: falsehood and lying, invidious craft and cruelty, all beastly and sensual practices, with idleness and sloth, are sins condemned by the light of nature. For these were the Cretans taxed by their own poets. <div eID="gen32615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32616" type="x-p"/> 3. Here is the verification of this by the apostle himself: <reference osisRef="Titus.1.13">v. 13</reference>. This witness is true, The apostle saw too much ground for that character. The temper of some nations is more inclined to some vices than others. The Cretans were too generally such as here described, slothful and ill-natured, false and perfidious, as the apostle himself vouches. And thence, <div eID="gen32616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32617" type="x-p"/> 4. He instructs Titus how to deal with them: <hi type="italic">Wherefore rebuke them sharply.</hi> When Paul wrote to Timothy he bade him instruct with meekness; but now, when he writes to Titus, he bids him rebuke them sharply. The reason of the difference may be taken from the different temper of Timothy and Titus; the former might have more keenness in his disposition, and be apt to be warm in reproving, whom therefore he bids to rebuke with meekness; and the latter might be one of more mildness, therefore he quickens him, and bids him rebuke sharply. Or rather it was from the difference of the case and people: Timothy had a more polite people to deal with, and therefore he must rebuke them with meekness; and Titus had to do with those who were more rough and uncultivated, and therefore he must rebuke them sharply; their corruptions were many and gross, and committed without shame or modesty, and therefore should be dealt with accordingly. There must in reproving be a distinguishing between sins and sins; some are more gross and heinous in their nature, or in the manner of their commission, with openness and boldness, to the greater dishonour of God and danger and hurt to men: and between sinners and sinners; some are of a more tender and tractable temper, apter to be wrought on by gentleness, and to be sunk and discouraged by too much roughness and severity; others are more hardy and stubborn, and need more cutting language to beget in them remorse and shame. Wisdom therefore is requisite to temper and manage reproofs aright, as may be most likely to do good. <reference osisRef="Jude.1.22-Jude.1.23">Jude 22, 23</reference>, <hi type="italic">Of some have compassion, making a difference; and others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire.</hi> The Cretans' sins and corruptions were many, great, and habitual; therefore they must be rebuked sharply. But that such direction might not be misconstrued, <div eID="gen32617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32618" type="x-p"/> 5. Here is the end of it noted: <hi type="italic">That they may be sound in the faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth;</hi> that is, that they may be and show themselves truly and effectually changed from such evil tempers and manners as those Cretans in their natural state lived in, and may not adhere to nor regard (as some who were converted might be too ready to do) the Jewish traditions and the superstitions of the Pharisees, which would be apt to make them disrelish the gospel, and the sound and wholesome truths of it. Observe, (1.) The sharpest reproofs must aim at the good of the reproved: they must not be of malice, nor hatred, nor ill-will, but of love; not to gratify pride, passion, nor any evil affection in the reprover, but to reclaim and reform the erroneous and the guilty. (2.) Soundness in the faith is most desirable and necessary. This is the soul's health and vigour, pleasing to God, comfortable to the Christian, and what makes ready to be cheerful and constant in duty. (3.) A special means to soundness in the faith is to turn away the ear from fables and the fancies of men (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1 Tim. i. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, that minister questions rather than godly edifying, which is in faith.</hi> So <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">ch. iv. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">Refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather to godliness.</hi> Fancies and devices of men in the worship of God are contrary to truth and piety. Jewish ceremonies and rites, that were at first divine appointments, the substance having come and their season and use being over, are now but unwarranted commands of men, which not only stand not with, but turn from, the truth, the pure gospel truth and spiritual worship, set up by Christ instead of that bodily service under the law. (4.) A fearful judgment it is to be turned away from the truth, to leave Christ for Moses, the spiritual worship of the gospel for the carnal ordinances of the law, or the true divine institutions and precepts for human inventions and appointments. <hi type="italic">Who hath bewitched you</hi> (said Paul to the Galatians, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.1">ch. iii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.3">3</reference>) <hi type="italic">that you should not obey the truth? Having begun in the Spirit, are you made perfect by the flesh?</hi> Thus having shown the end of sharply reproving the corrupt and vicious Cretans, that they might be sound in the faith, and not heed Jewish fables and commands of men, <div eID="gen32618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32619" type="x-p"/> 6. He gives the reasons of this, from the liberty we have by the gospel from legal observances, and the evil and mischief of a Jewish spirit under the Christian dispensation in the <reference osisRef="Titus.15 Titus.16">last two verses</reference>. To good Christians that are sound in the faith and thereby purified <hi type="italic">all things are pure.</hi> Meats and drinks, and such things as were forbidden under the law (the observances of which some still maintain), in these there is now no such distinction, <hi type="italic">all are pure</hi> (lawful and free in their use), <hi type="italic">but to those that are defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure;</hi> things lawful and good they abuse and turn to sin; they suck poison out of that from which others draw sweetness; their mind and conscience, those leading faculties, being defiled, a taint is communicated to all they do. <hi type="italic">The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Prov. xv. 8</reference>. And <reference osisRef="Prov.21.4">ch. xxi. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">The ploughing of the wicked is sin,</hi> not in itself, but as done by him; the carnality of the mind and heart mars all the labour of the hand. <div eID="gen32619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32620" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Objection.</hi> But are not these judaizers (as you call them) men who profess religion, and speak well of God, and Christ, and righteousness of life, and should they be so severely taxed? <hi type="italic">Answer, They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and to every good work reprobate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.16">v. 16</reference>. There are many who in word and tongue profess to know God, and yet in their lives and conversations deny and reject him; their practice is a contradiction to their profession. <hi type="italic">They come unto thee as the people cometh, and they sit before thee as my people, and they hear thy words, but they will not do them: with their mouth they show much love, but their heart goeth after their covetousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">Ezek. xxxiii. 31</reference>. <hi type="italic">Being abominable, and disobedient, and to every good work reprobate.</hi> The apostle, instructing Titus to rebuke sharply, does himself rebuke sharply; he gives them very hard words, yet doubtless no harder than their case warranted and their need required. <hi type="italic">Being abominable</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">bdelyktoi,</hi></hi> deserving that God and good men should turn away their eyes from them as nauseous and offensive. <hi type="italic">And disobedient</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">apeitheis,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">unpersuadable</hi> and <hi type="italic">unbelieving.</hi> They might do divers things; but it was not the obedience of faith, nor what was commanded, or short of the command. <hi type="italic">To every good work reprobate,</hi> without skill or judgment to do any thing aright. See the miserable condition of hypocrites, such as have a form of godliness, but without the power; yet let us not be so ready to fix this charge on others as careful that it agree not to ourselves, that there be not in us <hi type="italic">an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God;</hi> but that we be <hi type="italic">sincere and without offence till the day of Christ, being filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are by Jesus Christ unto the glory and praise of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.10-Phil.1.11">Phil. i. 10, 11</reference>.  <chapter eID="Titus.1"/> <div eID="gen32620" type="x-p"/>

entries.a76b2834ef2c2e71833c94b604ad8d25be8cc653: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18251"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen37863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Genuineness.--</hi>Clement of Rome quotes it [Epistle to the Corinthians, 2]; Irenæus [Against Heresies, 3.3.4] refers to it as Paul's; Theophilus of Antioch [To Autolychus, 3.14], quotes it as Scripture. Compare Clement of Alexandria [Miscellanies, 1, p. 299]; Tertullian [The Prescription against Heretics, 6].<div eID="gen37863" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37862" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Time and Place of Writing.--</hi>This Epistle seems to have been written from Corinth [Birks], subsequently to his first imprisonment, when Paul was on his way to Nicopolis (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>) in Epirus, where he purposed passing the winter, shortly before his martyrdom, A.D. 67. Birks thinks, from the similarity of the Epistle to Titus and First Timothy, that both were written from the same place, Corinth, and at dates not widely apart; First Timothy shortly after coming to Corinth, before he had planned a journey to Epirus, the Epistle to Titus afterwards. The journey to Crete and Ephesus for the bearers of his letters would be easy from Corinth, and he could himself thence easily pass into Epirus. He had shortly before visited Crete, wherein a Church existed (though without due organization), the first foundation of which he may have partly laid at his former visit (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.7">Ac 27:7</reference>, &c.), when on his way to his first imprisonment at Rome. That he returned to the East after his first imprisonment appears most probable from <reference osisRef="Phil.2.24">Php 2:24</reference>; Phm 22. However, there may have been seeds of Christianity sown in Crete, even before his first visit, by the Cretans who heard Peter's preaching on Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.11">Ac 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Occasion of Writing.--</hi>Corrupt elements soon showed themselves in the Cretan Church, similar to those noticed in the Epistles to Timothy, as existing in the Ephesian Church, Judaism, false pretensions to science, and practical ungodliness. Paul, on his late visit, had left Titus in Crete to establish Church government, and ordain presbyters (deacons are not mentioned). Titus had been several times employed by Paul on a mission to the Corinthian Churches, and had probably thence visited Crete, which was within easy reach of Corinth. Hence the suitableness of his selection by the apostle for the superintendence of the Cretan Church. Paul now follows up with instructions by letter those he had already given to Titus in person on the qualifications of elders, and the graces becoming the old, the young, and females, and warns him against the unprofitable speculations so rife in Crete. The national character of the Cretans was low in the extreme, as Epimenides, quoted in <reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>, paints it. Livy [History, 44.45], stigmatizes their avarice; Polybius [Histories, 6.46.9], their ferocity and fraud; and [Histories, 6.47.5], their mendacity, so much so, that "to Cretanize" is another name for to lie: they were included in the proverbial three infamous initials "K" or "C," "Cappadocia, Crete, Cilicia."<div eID="gen37865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Notices of Titus.--</hi>It is strange that he is never mentioned by this name in Acts, and there seems none of those mentioned in that book who exactly answers to him. He was a Greek, and therefore a Gentile (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.1">Ga 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>), and converted by Paul (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.4">Tit 1:4</reference>). He accompanied the apostle on the deputation sent from the Church of Antioch to Jerusalem, to consult the apostles respecting the circumcision of Gentile converts (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.2">Ac 15:2</reference>); and, agreeably to the decree of the council there, was not circumcised. He was in company with Paul at Ephesus, whence he was sent to Corinth to commence the collection for the Jerusalem saints, and to ascertain the effect of the First Epistle on the Corinthians (2Co 7:6-9; 8:<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">12:18</reference>), and there showed an unmercenary spirit. He next proceeded to Macedon, where he joined Paul, who had been already eagerly expecting him at Troas (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Co 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>, "Titus my brother," <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6">2Co 7:6</reference>). He was then employed by the apostle in preparing the collection for the poor saints in Judea, and became the bearer of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.16">2Co 8:16</reference>, 17, 23). Paul in it calls him "my partner and fellow helper concerning you." His being located in Crete (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">Tit 1:5</reference>) was subsequent to Paul's first imprisonment, and shortly before the second, about A.D. 67, ten years subsequent to the last notice of him in Second Corinthians (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">2Co 12:18</reference>), A.D. 57. He probably met Paul, as the apostle desired, at Nicopolis; for his subsequent journey into Dalmatia, thence (or else from Rome, whither he may have accompanied Paul) would be more likely, than from the distant Crete (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>, written subsequently to the Epistle to Titus). In the unsettled state of things then, Titus' episcopal commission in Crete was to be but temporary, Paul requiring the presence of Titus with himself, whenever Artemas or Tychicus should arrive in Crete and set him free from his duties there.<div eID="gen37866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37867" type="x-p"/> Tradition represents him to have died peaceably in Crete, as archbishop of Gortyna, at an advanced age.<div eID="gen37867" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Titus.1.1-Titus.1.16">Tit 1:1-16</reference>. Address: For What End Titus Was Left in Crete. Qualifications for Elders: Gainsayers in Crete Needing Reproof.</title> <div sID="gen37868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18251"/><hi type="bold">1. servant of God--</hi>not found elsewhere in the same connection. In <reference osisRef="Rom.1.1">Ro 1:1</reference> it is "servant of Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Ga 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.16.17">Ac 16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Re 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">15:3</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rom.1.1">Ro 1:1</reference>, there follows, "called to be an apostle," which corresponds to the general designation of the office first, "servant of God," here, followed by the special description, "apostle of Jesus Christ." The full expression of his apostolic office answers, in both Epistles, to the design, and is a comprehensive index to the contents. The peculiar form here would never have proceeded from a forger.<div eID="gen37868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the faith--</hi>rather, "for," "with a view to subserve the faith"; this is the object of my apostleship (compare <reference osisRef="Titus.1.4">Tit 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.5">Ro 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the elect--</hi>for whose sake we ought to endure all things (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.10">2Ti 2:10</reference>). This election has its ground, not in anything belonging to those thus distinguished, but in the purpose and will of God from everlasting (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.30-Rom.8.33">Ro 8:30-33</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.18.7">Lu 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.12">Col 3:12</reference>). <reference osisRef="Acts.13.48">Ac 13:48</reference> shows that all faith on the part of the elect, rests on the divine foreordination: they do not become elect by their faith, but receive faith, and so become believers, because they are elect.<div eID="gen37870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the acknowledging of the truth--</hi>"and (for promoting) the full knowledge of the truth," that is, the Christian truth (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after godliness--</hi>that is, which belongs to piety: opposed to the knowledge which has not for its object the truth, but error, doctrinal and practical (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>); or even which has for its object mere earthly truth, not growth in the divine life. "Godliness," or "piety," is a term peculiar to the Pastoral Epistles: a fact explained by the apostle having in them to combat doctrine tending to "ungodliness" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Ti 2:16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen37872" type="x-p"/>
entries.08cdf1ddddada407c8ce41977ee252a23581edf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18252"/><div sID="gen37873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18252"/><hi type="bold">2. In hope of eternal life--</hi>connected with the whole preceding sentence. That whereon rests my aim as an apostle to promote the elect's faith and full knowledge of the truth, is, "the hope of eternal life" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.23.6">Ac 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.15">24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.20">28:20</reference>).<div eID="gen37873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that cannot lie--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Ro 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.29">11:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">He 6:18</reference>).<div eID="gen37874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">promised before the world began--</hi>a contracted expression for "purposed before the world began (literally, 'before the ages of time'), and promised actually in time," the promise springing from the eternal purpose; as in <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>, the gift of grace was the result of the eternal purpose "before the world began." <div eID="gen37875" type="x-p"/>
entries.80b1d18c47629101e2823f09d458c2c6cbbe0217: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18253"/><div sID="gen37876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18253"/><hi type="bold">3. in due times--</hi>Greek, "in its own seasons," the seasons appropriate to it, and fixed by God for it (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen37876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">manifested--</hi>implying that the "promise," <reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">Tit 1:2</reference>, had lain hidden in His eternal purpose heretofore (compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen37877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his word--</hi>equivalent to "eternal life" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">Tit 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.24">Joh 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.63">6:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.3">17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen37878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through preaching--</hi>Greek, "in preaching," of rather as Alford (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>), "in the (Gospel) proclamation (the thing preached, the Gospel) with which I was entrusted."<div eID="gen37879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to--</hi>in pursuance of (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1Ti 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God our Saviour--</hi>rather as Greek, "of our Saviour God." God is predicated of our Saviour (compare Jude 25; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.47">Lu 1:47</reference>). Also <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Psa 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.12.2">Is 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">45:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">21</reference>, Septuagint. Applied to Jesus, <reference osisRef="Titus.1.4">Tit 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>. <div eID="gen37881" type="x-p"/>
entries.141865e6318dc5180cf1bfc0adc5fc23edee7041: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18254"/><div sID="gen37882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18254"/><hi type="bold">4. Titus, mine own son--</hi>Greek, "my genuine child" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Ti 1:2</reference>), that is, converted by my instrumentality (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">1Co 4:17</reference>; Phm 10).<div eID="gen37882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after the common faith--</hi>a genuine son in respect to (in virtue of) the faith common to all the people of God, comprising in a common brotherhood Gentiles as well as Jews, therefore embracing Titus a Gentile (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.1">2Pe 1:1</reference>; Jude 3).<div eID="gen37883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Grace, mercy, and peace--</hi>"mercy" is omitted in some of the oldest manuscripts. But one of the best and oldest manuscripts supports it (compare Notes, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Ti 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.2">2Ti 1:2</reference>). There are many similarities of phrase in the Pastoral Epistles.<div eID="gen37884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read only "Christ Jesus."<div eID="gen37885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our Saviour--</hi>found thus added to "Christ" only in Paul's Pastoral Epistles, and in <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.1">2Pe 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>; 2:20; 3:18. <div eID="gen37886" type="x-p"/>
entries.468a257d5d1ac9323ed241a11f4c96926334a060: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18255"/><div sID="gen37887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18255"/><hi type="bold">5. I left thee--</hi>"I left thee behind" [Alford] when I left the island: not implying permanence of commission (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen37887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Crete--</hi>now Candia.<div eID="gen37888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set in order--</hi>rather as Greek, "that thou mightest follow up (the work begun by me), setting right the things that are wanting," which I was unable to complete by reason of the shortness of my stay in Crete. Christianity, doubtless, had long existed in Crete: there were some Cretans among those who heard Peter's preaching on Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.11">Ac 2:11</reference>). The number of Jews in Crete was large (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.10">Tit 1:10</reference>), and it is likely that those scattered in the persecution of Stephen (<reference osisRef="Acts.11.19">Ac 11:19</reference>) preached to them, as they did to the Jews of Cyprus, &c. Paul also was there on his voyage to Rome (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.7-Acts.27.12">Ac 27:7-12</reference>). By all these instrumentalities the Gospel was sure to reach Crete. But until Paul's later visit, after his first imprisonment at Rome, the Cretan Christians were without Church organization. This Paul began, and had commissioned (before leaving Crete) Titus to go on with, and now reminds him of that commission.<div eID="gen37889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ordain--</hi>rather, "appoint," "constitute."<div eID="gen37890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in every city--</hi>"from city to city."<div eID="gen37891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as I ... appointed thee--</hi>that is, as I directed thee; prescribing as well the act of constituting elders, as also the manner of doing so, which latter includes the qualifications required in a presbyter presently stated. Those called "elders" here are called "bishops" in <reference osisRef="Titus.1.7">Tit 1:7</reference>. Elder is the term of dignity in relation to the college of presbyters; bishop points to the duties of his office in relation to the flock. From the unsound state of the Cretan Christians described here, we see the danger of the want of Church government. The appointment of presbyters was designed to check idle talk and speculation, by setting forth the "faithful word." <div eID="gen37892" type="x-p"/>
entries.92a60a3730480fb3bf9146e8684dd9cba84bfc4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18256"/><div sID="gen37893" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18256"/>6. (Compare Notes, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2-1Tim.3.4">1Ti 3:2-4</reference>.) The thing dwelt on here as the requisite in a bishop, is a good reputation among those over whom he is to be set. The immorality of the Cretan professors rendered this a necessary requisite in one who was to be a reprover: and their unsoundness in doctrine also made needful great steadfastness in the faith (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.9">Tit 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen37893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having faithful children--</hi>that is, believing children. He who could not bring his children to faith, how shall he bring others? [Bengel]. Alford explains, "established in the faith."<div eID="gen37894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not accused--</hi>not merely not riotous, but "not (even) accused of riot" ("profligacy" [Alford]; "dissolute life" [Wahl]).<div eID="gen37895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unruly--</hi>insubordinate; opposed to "in subjection" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.4">1Ti 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen37896" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb80e33a66031ca3d98478e353b281477edf8e41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18257"/><div sID="gen37897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18257"/><hi type="bold">7. For ... must--</hi>The emphasis is on "must." The reason why I said "blameless," is the very idea of a "bishop" (an overseer of the flock; he here substitutes for "presbyter" the term which expresses his duties) involves the necessity for such blamelessness, if he is to have influence over the flock.<div eID="gen37897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">steward of God--</hi>The greater the master is, the greater the virtues required in His servant [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>); the Church is God's house, over which the minister is set as a steward (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.2-Heb.3.6">He 3:2-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1Pe 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">17</reference>). Note: ministers are not merely Church officers, but God's stewards; Church government is of divine appointment.<div eID="gen37898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not self-willed--</hi>literally, "self-pleasing"; unaccommodating to others; harsh, the opposite of "a lover of hospitality" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>); so Nabal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1-1Sam.25.44">1Sa 25:1-44</reference>); self-loving and imperious; such a spirit would incapacitate him for leading a willing flock, instead of driving.<div eID="gen37899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not given to wine--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1Ti 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8">1Ti 3:8</reference>).<div eID="gen37900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not given to filthy lucre--</hi>not making the Gospel a means of gain (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1Ti 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8">8</reference>). In opposition to those "teaching for filthy lucre's sake" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">1Ti 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.2">1Pe 5:2</reference>). <div eID="gen37901" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff92bcd3925ae52f604cc39a25cc63c3dc0a40ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18258"/><div sID="gen37902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18258"/><hi type="bold">8. lover of hospitality--</hi>needed especially in those days (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.13">Ro 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">He 13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.9">1Pe 4:9</reference>; 3Jo 5). Christians travelling from one place to another were received and forwarded on their journey by their brethren.<div eID="gen37902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lover of good men--</hi>Greek, "a lover of (all that is) good," men or things (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Php 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen37903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sober--</hi>towards one's self; "discreet"; "self-restrained" [Alford], (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9">1Ti 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">just--</hi>towards "men."<div eID="gen37905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy--</hi>towards God (see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.10">1Th 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">temperate--</hi>"One having his passions, tongue, hand and eyes, at command" [Chrysostom]; "continent." <div eID="gen37907" type="x-p"/>
entries.665a230b5152e3603f6c36fb19ff0ce300bfff1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18259"/><div sID="gen37908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18259"/><hi type="bold">9. Holding fast--</hi>Holding firmly to (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">Mt 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.13">Lu 16:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the faithful--</hi>true and trustworthy (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word as he has been taught--</hi>literally, "the word (which is) according to the teaching" which he has received (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.6">1Ti 4:6</reference>, end; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.14">2Ti 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Translate as Greek, "to exhort in doctrine (instruction) which is sound"; sound doctrine or instruction is the element IN which his exhorting is to have place ...
